links.note: The Chronicle of Edessa lists the city's bishops without a break after 410. In 519 a bishop who accepted Chalcedon expelled the monks who refused it. Later the anti-Chalcedonian leader Jacob Baradaeus was consecrated bishop for Edessa.

links.named_in_text: syriac-edessa-nisibis relationsSummary ('Parent of ... the Syriac Orthodox Church') and legacy ('descend from this tradition'); syriac-orthodox-west-syriac-christianity relationsSummary ('Heir of the Syriac tradition's Roman side (Ephrem's Edessa)').
wants: Menze, Justinian and the Making of the Syrian Orthodox Church (2008), or Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972): both are named in Build/worlds/wsyr/Doc_02_Source_Ecology.md but neither has been consulted
drafter_flags: Wigram (pp. 25-26) says the Edessene church 'was merged in that ecclesiastical circle that developed into the Patriarchate of Antioch'. That supports the Edessa-to-Antioch line in general, not the Syriac Orthodox by name; a reviewer may judge Inferential-Thin more honest.
The link spans a gap: this entry ends in 410 and the Syriac Orthodox entry opens in 451. The bishops' list carries the see of Edessa across it.
Cowper's own note (chronicle file line 354) asks why the expelled monks were called 'Oriental' at Edessa; they may not all have been Edessenes.
John of Ephesus (Lives 49) has Jacob consecrated for Edessa while living at Constantinople; the wsyr Doc_02 notes he was consecrated in absentia. The note says 'for Edessa' for that reason.
The date 519 is computed from the Chronicle's Seleucid year 831 (entry 89-90, December); check the conversion.
links.change_reason: New: the Syriac text calls itself parent of the Syriac Orthodox Church; the vendored chronicle and John of Ephesus show the see of Edessa passing into the anti-Chalcedonian hierarchy.

prose_changes.old: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church; the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine passed into Arabic and back to Europe.
prose_changes.new: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church. Their translators later carried Greek philosophy and medicine into Arabic, and from there back to Europe.
prose_changes.reason: The translation movement into Arabic belongs to the 8th-9th-century heirs (the-church-of-the-east-under-persia's own legacy says so), not to this 200-410 community; the legacy field already says 'Centuries later'.

prose_changes.old: He wrote against Marcion, he was baptized in the Edessene church, and he ran a school whose hymns Ephraim would later complain were better than the orthodox ones - which is why Ephraim wrote hymns.
prose_changes.new: He wrote against Marcion, and he was baptized in the Edessene church. He and his school made hymns that Ephraim later accused of sweetening poison for the simple, and Ephraim answered them with hymns of his own.
prose_changes.reason: Ephraim's own words (Hymns against Heresies 53, quoted in npnf213 lines 11241-11244: 'He blended for the simple poison with sweetness') complain of sweetened poison, not of better hymns. 'Which is why Ephraim wrote hymns' overstates: Gwynn notes (npnf213 11220-11232) that Ephraim's Nisibene hymns of c. 350 predate the controversy. Sozomen III.16 and Theodoret IV.26 support the answer in kind.

prose_changes.old: raised in a Jewish-Christian baptizing sect before breaking with it
prose_changes.new: raised in a sect of baptizers before breaking with it
prose_changes.reason: The vendored evidence (the Fihrist as summarised by Newman, npnf104 lines 828-829 and 943) shows Mani's father joined the Mugtasila ('Baptizers') and that Mani was told to leave his father's religion. That the sect was Jewish-Christian rests on the Cologne Mani Codex, which is neither vendored nor cited in the repo.

prose_changes.old: broke from the Jewish-Christian sect that raised him
prose_changes.new: broke from the sect of baptizers that raised him

prose_changes.old: In the East it lasted far longer: it was for a time the state religion of the Uyghur Khaganate from the 760s, and persisted in southern China for many centuries.

escalations: Grading call for Mark: the Syriac Orthodox and Persian-church links are drafted Widely Accepted on Wigram (1910), whose wording supports the Edessene parentage only in general terms. If that is judged too thin, both drop to Inferential-Thin, which would display a well-known descent as thin.

The brief's no-entry rule forced two true but unsourced claims out of the Manichaeism text ('Jewish-Christian' sect; Uyghur state religion from the 760s). Both are standard scholarship. Mark may prefer to vendor a source rather than soften the text.
